Got Land? : l’humour autochtone sous tou: Got Land?: Indigenous Humour in All Its Forms
« L’humour autochtone est unique, drôle: “Indigenous humour is unique, funny and informative. But hey, some of us are just telling jokes”
Le collectif Got Land? à Kahnawà:ke, ave: The Got Land? collective in Kahnawà:ke, with Trevor Thompson, Mike Bombay, Jenn Hayward, Janelle Niles and Randy Schmucker (left to right) Photo: Fatima Bah
<em>“I stole the white man’s suit cuz he: “I stole the white man’s suit cuz he stole my land,” says Janelle Niles, dressed in a purple suit and tie, in a Kahnawà:ke restaurant in front of a mostly Indigenous audience. The Afro-Indigenous comedian is performing in a show called Got Land?.
Accompagnée de plusieurs comédiens autoc: Joined by several Indigenous comedians and one non-Indigenous comedian, the troupe performs sketches and sets about Bill 96, colonialism, racism, fake Indigenous people, stolen land, and Two-Spirit and queer realities. Sitting around a table before hitting the road to visit other nations of Turtle Island (a term used by some Indigenous peoples to refer to North America), the comedians explain to us why positive, humorous initiatives like Got Land? are needed.
« L’humour autochtone est unique, drôle: “Indigenous humour is unique, funny and informative. But hey, some of us are just telling jokes,” reads <l1>the collective’s website</l1>. Rooted in Indigenous culture and customs for decades, humour is often a way to call out injustice or to teach life lessons. La Converse talked about it with the group of comedians. “Humour is part of our culture, it’s so unique! In our communities, we tease each other all the time, it’s like we’re all comedians. We’re always laughing and it’s a lot of fun,” says Janelle Niles, sitting down with La Converse after her show.
Son collègue Randy Schmucker, le plus je: Her colleague Randy Schmucker, the youngest member of the troupe, agrees. “It’s something I’ve studied and talked about with a lot of people. Humour is part of our tradition and it’s found throughout our history. We have jokes about society; there are people who are there to tell jokes or just to stir up trouble,” says the Anishnabe comedian. In a non-Indigenous context, this kind of humour isn’t always understood. So don’t be surprised if your Indigenous friends tease you a lot.
<strong>Changer l’image des Autochtones: Changing the image of Indigenous people through humour
En passant par l’humour, <em>Got Land?</: Through humour, Got Land? wants to change the image of Indigenous communities across Turtle Island. The collective’s founder, Janelle Niles, came up with the idea in 2019. Originally from Nova Scotia, she now lives in Ottawa. At her first open mic in Ottawa, the comedian quickly noticed the lack of diversity on stages in the nation’s capital.
« J’ai réalisé qu’il n’y avait qu’un hum: “I realized there was only one Black or Indigenous comedian in the whole show. I said to myself, ‘That can’t be, there have to be more Indigenous people here!’” says the Mi’kmaq comedian. Inspired by Toronto comedian Kenny Robinson, who created a comedy collective with a group of Black comedians, The Nubian Disciples All-Black Comedy Revue, Janelle decided to start her own troupe. Early in her career, when she got on stage in white spaces, the audience didn’t listen to her. “When we did this kind of Indigenous comedy at open mics and I dressed normally, people didn’t laugh, they didn’t pay me any attention,” says Janelle. “I told myself, ‘People listen to Black comedians all the time, they share the same stories I do, but I don’t get the same reception.’ So I started wearing a jacket and tie and boom! I started getting the laughs I deserved. Because now that I’m smart enough to be listened to, I’m no longer threatening.”
Sur scène, Janelle parle de son rapport: On stage, Janelle talks about her relationship with French, her upbringing, her relationship with her parents and her identity as a Black and Indigenous woman. Her sketches are political. “I was born Black and Indigenous, so I was born political. Every day, every second, I have to fight. I have to say what we live through, because that’s how I grew up,” says the comedian, adding that her mother often talked to her about Malcolm X and Martin Luther King.
« Lorsque je reprends le contrôle de mon: “As I take back control of my Indigenous identity, it becomes more important for me to be able to do this kind of humour, because we’ve tried to be humble and quiet for too long, but not anymore!” Janelle says emphatically, smiling. Her colleagues nod in agreement.
Dans le spectacle, on entend des comédie: The show features comedians from several nations: Janelle Niles, who is Mi’kmaq; Jenn Hayward, who is Métis; Randy Schmucker, who is Anishinabe; and Mike Bombay, who is Ojibwe.
On y trouve aussi Trevor Thompson, un ho: It also features Trevor Thompson, a white English-speaking man. In his set, the comedian talks about racism, conspiracy theories and the media. “Is Canada racist? We asked 25 white people,” he says, poking fun at polls in major Canadian media, in front of a welcoming crowd. At each show, the group invites a non-Indigenous comedian on stage. Creator Janelle Niles explains this approach. “At our first show, we had a special guest who wasn’t Indigenous. The audience loved him so much that we decided to invite a non-Indigenous comedian to every show. It’s not always the same people,” she says. And this decision is not trivial, the troupe insists. “Given the rise of the far right, putting on a show like ours with an all-Indigenous troupe can be seen as reverse racism. Which we’re not doing,” Janelle is quick to point out.
« C’est notre façon d’embaucher la diver: “It’s our way of hiring diversity,” she jokes. “I want to make sure my show is as inclusive as possible within Indigenous communities.” Young comedian Randy Schmucker is Anishnabe and European. “I’m Indigenous, but I’m also gay and vegan. That also makes me a threat to my traditional white family,” he says in the intro to his set. He goes on to talk about “pretendians” (people who falsely claim Indigenous identity) and about his queer identity. “I found out I was gay watching Pocahontas. There was something about John Smith,” says the comedian to a roaring audience. “All my life, I’ve been trying to find the answer to an old question: what makes the red man red? And I realized that when I’m on a date with a white man and he corrects me on my knowledge of First Nations history and culture, that’s what makes the red man red. And I guess that’s kind of how I feel when I’m on a date with my professor,” Randy continues in his set. For the troupe’s comedians, with his raw humour and quick wit, Randy represents the future of Indigenous humour and of decolonization. “I’d say I represent a face of intersection, not necessarily that of decolonization,” the comedian himself clarifies.
« J’ai beaucoup d’expériences uniques en: “I have a lot of unique experiences as an Indigenous queer person who grew up in an urban setting.” In Got Land?, the comedian says he feels valued for who he is. “I don’t have to prove my Indigenous and queer identity to anyone,” he tells us. Jenn Hayward is the “auntie,” the aunt, the mentor of the group. In her set, the Métis comedian from Saskatchewan talks about her relationship with her kids and her husband, as well as her privileges and French. “I’m a Métis woman from Saskatchewan, I grew up in a city and there are privileges I have that others don’t.
Alors, je ne monte pas sur scène pour re: So I don’t get on stage to represent something I’m not, especially with the pretendian trend,” the comedian explains. “I know a lot of things about the culture because of my upbringing, but that doesn’t make me a First Nations person, I’m still Métis. And I think that’s an important distinction, especially in Quebec,” she tells us. The troupe’s mentor has been doing comedy for several years. For her, being a comedian is a way of using her voice. “Part of that voice is the angry one, but I’m not at that stage anymore. I’ve been a victim of so many things in my life.
Je suis à un stade où je veux juste fair: I’m at a stage where I just want to tell jokes, and that’s where I’ve ended up in my comedy career,” she says candidly. The mother of three believes it’s important to show a diversity of voices in the show. With each of their performances, the comedians represent a part of their community, which is why the diversity of their experiences and of the nations they belong to matters.
Tout au long du spectacle, les comédiens: Throughout the show, the comedians, who come from elsewhere in Canada, talked about <l1>Bill 96</l1> and described how they see it as Indigenous people. On stage, Janelle Niles explains that she grew up in Nova Scotia, where French wasn’t taught until Grade 4. Once she got to Ottawa, where it was taught earlier, she didn’t understand the language. She ended up finishing high school without a single French credit. The comedian resisted and in fact studied Japanese for three years, which allowed her to graduate.
« Nous devons résister. Nous ne connaiss: “We have to resist. We don’t even know our own language, Mi’kmaq is dying,” she tells the audience, expressing her solidarity with the Mohawk Nation, which disagrees with the Act respecting French, the official and common language of Quebec. In an interview, the comedian explains her position. “Francophones immigrated here and they’re not on their land, they’re guests on our land. Why are they including us in this issue? We have other issues to deal with, like intergenerational trauma and the loss of our own languages. [...] I understand that they want to protect their culture, but they need to remember they’re guests on our land and that means listening to us first,” she says. Jenn Hayward explains why Bill 96 is part of the show.
« Nous n’avions pas entendu parler de la: “We hadn’t heard about the law before we did the show in Quebec a month ago. People here told us it was important to talk about it, so we looked into it. We’re not here to offend people; we’re not from here. But it’s okay to laugh at Bill 96, it’s comedy.” Coming from Western Canada, Jenn Hayward says she understands the goal of Bill 96. “We don’t learn anything about Quebec history, and I come from a place where we don’t learn much about Quebec,” she admits. But language remains an important part of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada’s work and, in her view, Bill 96 ignores that.
« Tu peux protéger tes droits, mais tu n: “You can protect your rights, but you don’t have to erase other people’s, and that’s what this law does. Yet if we, the comedians, went on stage and said screw white people, it wouldn’t be funny anymore. They would react negatively. If you don’t do anything with kindness and love, you can’t do anything,” says Jenn Hayward.

Avec <em>Got Land?</em>, le collectif so: With Got Land?, the collective wants to pave the way for Indigenous comedians and change perceptions of the nations of Turtle Island. The troupe’s elder, Jenn, praises Janelle, without whom this project wouldn’t have been possible. What advice does the troupe have for aspiring Indigenous comedians?
« Ça n’a pas été facile pour moi et plus: “It hasn’t been easy for me and many of us to do this work, and that’s why we exist.
Aujourd’hui, nous sommes là pour nous en: Today, we’re here to help each other. Reach out to us, we want to hear your voices, I’ll do everything I can to help you,” concludes Janelle Niles.
